comments.text: 19:22 19:22 my mom was a registered nurse for 40+ years. There was an older gentleman that ended up in her ward constantly and was so mean to the nurses. My mom got him as a patient one night and realized that he spoke Polish.  We were raised speaking in Polish. So instead of going in there and matching his energy like the other nurse did, the first time he rang the call bell she went in and let him air his grievances. Then calmly she walked over to him and petted his head while brushing his hair and said in Polish everything‘s going to be OK little duck.  Which doesn’t really translate into English properly, but it’s basically calling someone a baby but everything will be OK. But it’s something you would only say to a child.  He laughed for the first time ever and every time that his chronic illness would flare up and he would end up on that ward again he would always ask for my mother. After that he was always kinder to all of the nurses.  Humor, combined with professionalism and compassion AND timing I believe is half the battle when it comes to healing. The best healthcare workers realize that patients don’t want to be seen or identified by their charts they want to be seen for who they are and their roots. My mom is retired now, but she still tells that story and smiles every time.  She was with him when he passed and I’m so glad that she was on the Night Shift that evening. Not so much as a nurse but as a friend.  ❤ Anyone that reads this and is in the healthcare system, especially in America thank you so much for everything that you do. You’re not paid enough and the system is chronically and aggressively working against you. You are angels that walk among us. ❤

comments.text: So, IT professional here with about 13 years of experience, including some in a hospital. Most networks do have intranets, including hospitals. However with the way Epic and other EMR systems work, they are connected to the internet. A lot of the PCs, especially in EDs where you get a lot of login traffic from medical staff, are just something known as thin clients. They are a computer that only has a few small programs on it and when you log in, you aren't logging in to the computer but to a server in another area of the network that basically keeps all your programs and and info up so you don't have to clog every computer with every nurse and doctor's profile and so that the medical professionals and go from one computer to another with all the charts still up and never losing any work unless the server goes down. The reason they would shut everything down in a situation like this is because there is a possibility of that server getting compromised so until that is cleared and safe, they would shut it down/fully isolate it to patch and make any needed changes to try and keep it safe

comments.text: Hello Dr. Mike, healthcare IT/Informatics here, yes and no intranet is a thing and could be utilized to provide communication amongst departments. Many hospitals only use intranet as a policy form database and not as a communication hub. However, most EHRs are not internal and require direct external connection to work. Phones, pneumatic tube systems, pyxis machines, alaris pumps, e-prescribe, charting, imaging/PACs, are almost always using some external internet service to function. After watching this episode I asked my security team what they would do and they said they would probably do the same and turn off the external connections and lock down all computers onsite to prevent a cyberattack. One thing to note is cyberattacks can happen even in person, if an unauthorized person gains access to a network computer. First level access is a huge concern and is rarely thought about when talking about cybersecurity.

comments.text: Nursing in general is experiencing a massive shortage because of a combination of factors… There’s been a sharp increase in violence against clinical staff and excess burden on acute and emergent care (people using the ER instead of primary care). Also less funding of hospitals and clinical due to losses from Medicaid and Medicare cuts. Boomer and Gen Xer nurses are retiring. Also there are more education requirements, along with cuts to education funding, so it’s harder to get into clinical roles. There are stricter standards for ongoing education, which is needed for professional development but it sometimes means that nurses are off the floor to attend trainings. Speciality programs like SANE require extra training. And there are lots of regulatory requirements from independent orgs like The Joint Commission and Departments of Health. It’s having a cascading effect on healthcare and the public isn’t aware of how complicated the reasons are

comments.text:
Like some other comments have pointed out (but with maybe a little more information):

External access can be cut off in a situation like this in a number of ways, the big 'oh no we in trouble' option being pulling the connections from your primary network switches that actually connect you to the internet. At that point you are isolated. 

The problem is that once you've been infected most modern ransomware does not need you to remain connected to the internet to do it's thing. The infection is there and it's spreading. But these things are also designed to operate as quietly as possible until the moment it starts encrypting your files. Once that starts the only way to be 'safe' is to shut everything down then bring things back up in a controlled fashion so that the IT department can then begin damage assessment and control. 

The hospital that was already hit? Nothing you can do. The Intranet is already compromised. 

The PITT? Shutting down all the tech IS premature considering they could just pull their external lines (or depending on how robust their IT staffing and controls are) isolate their servers and machines on various subnets to leave some external functions in place while keeping their more important operations isolated. That being said in my experience IT in the medical world is vastly understaffed and underfunded like just about everything else in healthcare. 

Hell they might not even have good backups which would be a big argument in favor of the total shutdown (and firings after the fact)

comments.text:
@DoctorMike - I work in healthcare IT, and I'll take a stab at your query towards the end.

There are two ways your hospital gets its EMR suite. In the past, the safer and more expensive way was an on-premise deployment, where the infrastructure was paid for and deployed within the boundaries of the hospital itself. You might call this an intranet-style deployment.

Modern deployments are mostly cloud-based. This means that the software is centrally deployed for many clients on cloud providers such as Amazon, Google, etc. This is where AWS comes into play, for example. These deployments are significantly cheaper, but they can only interface with local hospital infrastructure (such as medical devices) through the public internet.

While I agree that some infrastructure could be local-only and could have run independently, purely local infrastructure is probably getting phased out.

Hope this helps.
